findings.evidence: Also, you submit the request in the portal. Countersign the employee request within two business days. You track its status there until the payment clears.
findings.fix: Split the paragraph by reader: state what the employee does (submit, track status) separately from what the approver does (countersign within two business days), naming the approver explicitly instead of leaving 'countersign' addressed to an unspecified 'you'.
findings.violation: The paragraph addresses two identifiably different readers, the employee submitting the request and the approver who countersigns it, as the same second-person 'you' with no separation, so the reader cannot tell whether countersigning is their own task or someone else's.

findings.evidence: Employees record the stipend item on the request form. Finance reconciles the reimbursable item against the request log each month. Payroll releases the covered purchase amount after that monthly review.
findings.fix: Pick one term, such as equipment item, for the purchase being reimbursed and use it in place of stipend item, reimbursable item, and covered purchase amount throughout this section.
findings.violation: Three different terms, stipend item, reimbursable item, and covered purchase amount, are used across three consecutive sentences for what appears to be the single thing the employee bought and is being reimbursed for, with no defined-terms signal that the three are the same.

findings.evidence: the stipend request, once the manager signs it, after finance confirms the budget line, moves to final processing (How to Apply); The manager reviews the request within two business days (Approval Timeline); Countersign the employee request within two business days (Terminology Notes); The finance office reviews every stipend request over 200 dollars before it pays out (Review Responsibility).
findings.fix: Consolidate the manager sign-off, the countersignature step, the budget confirmation, and the finance review threshold into a single Approval section the reader can read start to finish.
findings.location: How to Apply; Approval Timeline; Terminology Notes; Review Responsibility
findings.violation: The approval process, manager sign-off, countersignature step, and the finance review threshold for larger requests are split across four sections that are not adjacent and do not reference each other, so a reader who needs the full approval sequence before applying has to assemble it from across the whole document rather than from one place.

findings.evidence: The benefits team coordinates every stipend request from intake to payout.
findings.fix: Rewrite the opening sentence to state the topic the rest of the paragraph covers.
findings.violation: The paragraph's opening sentence shares almost no vocabulary with the rest of the paragraph, so it does not preview the paragraph's actual topic.

findings.evidence: The benefits team coordinates every stipend request from intake to payout. A separate audit last spring reviewed unrelated travel expenses. Federal guidance on remote work continues to evolve each year. The office coffee budget was reset at the start of the quarter.
findings.fix: Remove the audit, federal-guidance, and coffee-budget sentences from this section, or move each to its own relevant section, so Program Coordination states only what it coordinates.
findings.violation: The section pursues four unrelated themes, stipend coordination, a past travel-expense audit, federal remote-work guidance, and the office coffee budget, with no signal connecting them, so a reader finishing the section cannot state what it was actually about.

findings.evidence: The benefits team publishes the equipment catalog on the first business day of the month. Every entry carries a date stamp so the record stays easy to audit. (Program Overview) / The IT asset group updates the equipment catalog after every open enrollment period. Every entry carries a date stamp so the record stays easy to audit. (Special Cases)
findings.fix: State the equipment catalog's full publishing and update cadence, by both the benefits team and the IT asset group, in one place in Program Overview.
findings.violation: Governance of the equipment catalog, who maintains it and on what schedule, is split between Program Overview and a later Special Cases section under an identical repeated sentence, so a reader has to find and reconcile two separated sections to learn who actually controls the catalog and when.

findings.evidence: Also, the stipend request, once the manager signs it, after finance confirms the budget line, moves to final processing.
findings.fix: Move the interrupting clause elsewhere, or split it into its own sentence.
findings.violation: 3 comma-set-off clause(s) totalling 14 words intervene between the sentence's apparent subject and its verb.

findings.evidence: An incomplete request pauses the timeline until the missing item arrives. The...
findings.fix: Open the paragraph with a transition word that states its relationship to the prior paragraph.
findings.violation: The paragraph opens with none of the fixed transition words, so the reader is not told how it relates to the paragraph before it.

findings.evidence: Completing the request begins with confirming eligibility, and the uploaded receipt.
findings.fix: Restate every item in the series with the same grammatical form.
findings.violation: The series' 2 items mix grammatical forms (gerund, other) at their head words instead of sharing one form.

findings.evidence: The finance office reviews every stipend request over 200 dollars before it pays out.
findings.fix: End the sentence on the threshold instead, for example: Before paying out, the finance office reviews every stipend request over 200 dollars.
findings.violation: The sentence's newest, most important element, the 200-dollar threshold that triggers extra review, is buried in the middle, while the sentence ends on before it pays out, information the reader already has from context.
